1065.title: How the Bible was gathered
1065.hook: letters passed hand to hand and read aloud, until the churches knew which books were theirs
1065.howItsDone: Christians receive the Bible as the books the church read and recognized in worship; Catholic and Orthodox Bibles include some Old Testament books that Protestant Bibles leave out or print separately as the Apocrypha.

segments.voice: Yesterday, four sides: scripture, tradition, reason and experience, with scripture as the ground. Your line was four sides of a question.

At the end of a letter to a small church in Colossae, Paul adds a note about the mail. When this letter has been read to you, he says, send it on to the church at Laodicea, and read the one from Laodicea too. A scroll, read aloud to a room of people, then rolled up and carried down the road to the next room. That's the Bible before it was a book. Day one hundred twenty-five called it a library. Today: how the Bible was gathered.

The Bible didn't arrive as a bound volume. Luke's Gospel opens by admitting there were other accounts: "Forasmuch as many have taken in hand to set forth in order a declaration of those things which are most surely believed among us." Many. Luke wasn't the only one writing, and the churches had to come to know which writings were theirs. Christians often describe it the way Paul's note suggests: by reading. The writings churches kept reading aloud, Sunday after Sunday, that they trusted as coming from the apostles and their circle, and that matched the faith they'd been taught, came to be called scripture. You can watch it start inside the Bible. The second letter of Peter mentions Paul's letters, which some people twist, "as they do also the other scriptures." Paul's mail, set beside the scriptures. Over time, bishops and councils wrote the books down in lists. One that survives is a letter Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria, sent his churches at Easter. He names the books of both testaments, calls them fountains of salvation, and adds that no one should add to them or take from them. Churches still differ on some books. Catholic and Orthodox Bibles include books such as Tobit and the Maccabees in the Old Testament; Protestant Bibles leave them out or print them apart, as the Apocrypha. Catholics and Orthodox stress the church recognizing the books; Protestants stress the books carrying their own authority, which the church came to see. Both say the church didn't invent the Bible. It listened, and kept reading.

Open a Bible, or a Bible app, to the contents page: a list, like the one Athanasius sent his churches. Read the names slowly, one at a time, Genesis, Ruth, Psalms, Mark, Romans, each one read aloud in rooms full of people long before it was printed there. If you pray, give thanks for the readers; if not, just let the names go by.
How the Bible was gathered: not voted into being in one afternoon, but read aloud in worship until the churches knew which books were theirs, and then written down in lists.

1066.title: What inspired means
1066.hook: all-scripture-is-God-breathed (2 Timothy 3:16) is read by some as word-for-word, by others as God working through human writers
1066.howItsDone: Christians call the Bible inspired, God-breathed; some, often evangelical, stress that its very words are without error, others stress God working through true human authors, and Catholic teaching affirms both.

segments.voice: Yesterday, how the Bible was gathered: letters read aloud in worship until the churches knew which books were theirs. Your line was the church read these.

Dust, shaped into a person, lying still on the ground. Not alive yet. Then, in the second chapter of Genesis, God leans close: "and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life; and man became a living soul." Dust, plus breath, equals someone. Hold that picture, because a short line in a letter that opens with Paul's name reaches for the same breath, and Christians read it in more than one way. Today's word: inspiration.

The word inspiration carries a picture of breath. The line is in the second letter to Timothy: "All scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness." Behind the King James phrase is a Greek word, theopneustos, usually rendered God-breathed. Genesis again: God breathes, and something lifeless comes alive. Notice what the verse spends its breath on. It doesn't explain how the breathing worked. It says what scripture is for: teaching, correcting, setting straight, training. It's written to Timothy, who, it says, has known the holy scriptures from a child. It's practical. The how is where Christians read differently. Some, often evangelical, stress that God guided the writers so closely that the very words are what God intended, and teach that the Bible is without error in all it affirms. Others put the weight on God working through human writers: their languages, styles, times and personalities. Catholic teaching holds the two together: God is the author of scripture, the human writers are true authors too, and the books teach without error the truth God wanted written down for our salvation. Orthodox and Protestant teachers stand at different points along that line. Both sides lean on a verse in the second letter of Peter: "holy men of God spake as they were moved by the Holy Ghost." Divine and human in the same sentence. Christians argue about how much weight each half carries. They agree on the breath: a book that, they say, didn't just get written. It got breathed into.

Breathe in, and on the out-breath say quietly: all scripture is given by inspiration of God. On the next out-breath: and is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness. Then just breathe, noticing that every word rode out on air; if you pray, ask that the words you read be alive for you, and if not, simply rest in the breath.
Inspiration. A breath word. In 2 Timothy, scripture is God-breathed, and useful for teaching and training.
Your line: god-breathed. Dust, and then breath, and then someone comes alive. See you tomorrow.

1067.title: Four senses
1067.hook: medieval readers found four layers: literal, allegorical, moral, and where it leads
1067.howItsDone: Catholic teaching names the literal sense and three spiritual senses of scripture; Orthodox preaching often draws on the early fathers' spiritual readings, and Protestant preaching, following the Reformers, stresses the plain sense of the text.

segments.voice: Yesterday, inspiration: scripture as God-breathed, like dust coming alive in Genesis. Your line was god-breathed.

How many meanings can one word hold? Try Jerusalem. To a pilgrim, it's a city on a hill, with walls and a temple. To a monk named John Cassian, writing for other monks, it could be four things at once: the earthly city, the church, the human soul, and the city of God waiting at the end of everything. One word, four rooms. For many medieval readers, that wasn't a trick. It was how you read the Bible carefully. Today's word: four senses.
screen: `A CITY, A CHURCH, A SOUL, HEAVEN.`

segments.voice: The four senses are four layers of meaning in a passage of scripture. The literal: what the words say and what happened. The allegorical: what it shows about Christ and the church. The moral: what it asks of you, how to live. And the one with the hardest name, the anagogical: where it leads, toward the end of all things and the life to come. A little Latin rhyme, tradition says, summed it up, roughly: the letter teaches what happened, allegory what to believe, the moral what to do, and the anagogy where you're going. There's a seed of it in the Bible itself. In Galatians, Paul tells of Abraham's two sons, one by Hagar the bondmaid and one by the freewoman, then says: "Which things are an allegory: for these are the two covenants." A family story, read as a story about God's promises. Medieval teachers also kept a rule. Thomas Aquinas taught that the other senses stand on the literal: you don't float off to heaven until you know what the text actually says. Churches have kept this differently. Catholic teaching still names the four senses. Orthodox readers draw deeply on the early fathers' spiritual readings. Reformers such as Luther and Calvin pushed hard for the plain sense, wary of allegories that could make a verse mean anything, while still reading Christ throughout the scriptures. All of them were asking the same thing: how deep does this go?

Take the shepherd who finds one sheep missing, goes after it, and carries it home on his shoulders, glad. Move through it slowly: see the hillside and the search; then the shepherd as Christ, seeking, as some readers have; then who has gone missing from your circle, and whether you'd go looking; then where it leads, since Jesus ends the story with joy in heaven. If you pray, stay in whichever layer feels like prayer.
Four senses. Literal, allegorical, moral, and where it leads: the medieval way of reading one passage on four floors at once.
Your line: layers of meaning. The literal comes first, and the rest stand on it. Until tomorrow.

1068.title: The way of not-knowing
1068.hook: Orthodox and mystics say what God is not, since God is beyond every idea
1068.howItsDone: Orthodox Christians speak of God both by what God is and, with special honor, by what God is not; in the West, contemplative Christians practice a similar wordless prayer, drawing on books like The Cloud of Unknowing.

segments.voice: Yesterday, four senses: what happened, what to believe, what to do, and where it leads. Your line was layers of meaning.

The mountain is wrapped in smoke and cloud, and the ground shakes with thunder. The people at the bottom have had enough. They step back and want Moses to speak to them instead of God. Then Exodus gives one quiet sentence: "And the people stood afar off, and Moses drew near unto the thick darkness where God was." Not into a blaze of light. Into the dark. Some Christians have read that sentence as a map for prayer: the closer you come to God, the less you can see. Today's word: apophatic.

Apophatic is usually explained from a Greek word for saying no. The apophatic way speaks of God by saying what God is not. Not a thing among other things. Not made. Not in one place. Not limited. Not the size of any idea we have. Each not clears away a picture that was too small. Its partner, the cataphatic way, says what God is: good, light, love. Orthodox teaching holds the two together, and gives the not-saying a place of honor; mystics in the West walked the same road. The Bible keeps both in view. God tells Moses, "Thou canst not see my face: for there shall no man see me, and live." A letter to Timothy speaks of God "dwelling in the light which no man can approach unto; whom no man hath seen, nor can see." Light so bright it works like darkness. Gregory of Nyssa, writing about the life of Moses, noticed the order of the story: Moses meets God first in light, at the burning bush, later in cloud, and at last in thick darkness. For Gregory, going deeper meant seeing less, and knowing more. In medieval England, an unknown writer made a small book of it, The Cloud of Unknowing. Its counsel, put simply: you won't reach God by thinking harder; reach into the cloud with love. None of this is the same as knowing nothing. It keeps God larger than your best idea, and lets silence say what words can't.

Whatever you believe, try this as an exercise: on each out-breath, set down one picture of God that's too small. Not an old man on a cloud, not a vending machine, not my worst fear, not my best idea either. When you run out, sit in the space that's left without filling it; if you pray, let that empty space be your prayer.
Apophatic. The way of not-knowing: speaking of God by saying what God is not, because God is beyond every idea.
Your line: more than you think. Silence can say it too. Same time tomorrow.

1069.title: All-powerful, all-loving
1069.hook: classic attributes: God is almighty, all-knowing, everywhere, and love
1069.howItsDone: In churches that use the Apostles' or Nicene Creed, congregations confess God as the Father Almighty, and preaching and hymns often pair God's power with God's love, drawing on Psalm 139 and the first letter of John.

segments.voice: Yesterday, apophatic: speaking of God by what God is not. Your line was more than you think.

"I believe in God the Father Almighty, Maker of heaven and earth." In churches that say the Apostles' Creed, a whole room says that line together, some half awake, some meaning every word. Almighty is one of the first things it says about God. Yesterday was the way of not. Today goes the other way, to the old list of what Christians say God is: almighty, all-knowing, everywhere, and love. Put the first word next to the last, and things get interesting. Today's word: all-powerful.
screen: `FROM WHAT GOD IS NOT, TO WHAT GOD IS.`

segments.voice: Christian teachers have long spoken of God's attributes, the things that are true of God. All-powerful: in Genesis, God says to Abram, "I am the Almighty God; walk before me, and be thou perfect." All-knowing and everywhere come alive in Psalm 139, which sounds less like a textbook than like someone who can't get away. "For there is not a word in my tongue, but, lo, O LORD, thou knowest it altogether." Then: "Whither shall I go from thy spirit? or whither shall I flee from thy presence?" Heaven, the grave, the far side of the sea: God is there too. And there the psalm turns: "Even there shall thy hand lead me, and thy right hand shall hold me." Being known everywhere stops being surveillance and becomes being held. Then the fourth word. The first letter of John says it plainly: "He that loveth not knoweth not God; for God is love." Notice the grammar. The Bible calls God almighty, but in this letter love is not just something God has or does. It's what God is. Some teachers read the whole list through that line: power that serves love, knowledge that loves what it knows, a presence that holds. And honesty matters here. Put all-powerful beside all-loving, then look at a hospital ward or a news feed, and hard questions appear. Christians have wrestled with them for a long time, and still do. The list doesn't answer every question. It tells you which word some Christians put first.

On one breath, almighty; on the next, all-knowing; then everywhere; then love; then go round again, slowly. Notice which word meets you today, and whether any of them unsettles you; both are worth noticing, and you don't have to explain why. If you pray, rest on the word that met you and stay with it.
All-powerful. Almighty, as the creed says, and in the first letter of John, held together with the line God is love.
Your line: god is love first. Power, in this reading, serves love. See you tomorrow.

1070.title: Pictures of the Trinity
1070.hook: the sun, its light and heat; a lover, a beloved, and love: every picture helps and falls short
1070.howItsDone: Christians baptize in the name of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, and teachers often use pictures like the sun or a shamrock to explain the Trinity, while saying that no picture is the reality.

segments.voice: Yesterday, all-powerful: almighty, all-knowing, everywhere, and love. Your line was god is love first.

A small green plant, three leaves on one stem. A story people tell says Saint Patrick, preaching in Ireland, bent down, picked a shamrock, and held it up: three leaves, one plant. Whether it happened, nobody can show. But the story keeps getting told, because it answers a real need. Christians say God is one, and God is Father, Son and Holy Spirit, and sooner or later somebody asks, how does that work? And somebody reaches for a picture. Today: pictures of the Trinity.

Day two hundred ninety-nine called the Trinity one God in three persons: Father, Son and Holy Spirit. The Bible doesn't give a diagram, but it keeps naming the three together. Jesus sends his friends out "baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost." In the name. One name, three. Paul ends a letter: "The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, and the love of God, and the communion of the Holy Ghost, be with you all." So teachers reached for pictures. One is the sun: the sun itself, its light, and the warmth that reaches your face. One sun, not three, and you never meet the light without the sun. Augustine reached for love, which needs someone who loves, someone who is loved, and the love between them: three, and one act of love. And there's Patrick's shamrock. Every one helps, and every one falls short. The sun can make the Son and the Spirit sound like products of the Father, less than him. The shamrock can make each person sound like a third of God. A popular picture, water as ice, liquid and steam, can make God sound like one person changing costumes, which the creeds reject. The old creed named after Athanasius warns against both mistakes: don't mix up the persons, and don't split the one God into pieces. So teachers keep using pictures, and keep letting them go. It's the way of not-knowing again: a picture opens the door, and then you walk past it.

Draw three overlapping circles, on paper, with a finger on the table, or in your mind, with one small shape in the middle where all three meet. Look at the middle, then at where the picture breaks: circles have edges, and Christians say God doesn't. Let the drawing help and fall short at once; if you pray, you can pray toward the middle.
Pictures of the Trinity. The sun and its light and warmth; a lover, a beloved and love; a shamrock. Each opens a door, and none is the room.
Your line: every picture falls short. Each one still opens a door. Rest well.

1071.title: The filioque
1071.hook: Western churches added and the Son to the creed about the Spirit; the Orthodox did not, and the argument continues gently
1071.howItsDone: Catholic, Anglican and other Western churches say in the Nicene Creed that the Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son; Orthodox churches say from the Father, keeping the creed's older wording.

segments.voice: Yesterday, pictures of the Trinity: the sun, a lover and love, a shamrock. Your line was every picture falls short.

Sunday morning, two churches on the same street. In one, the people say the Nicene Creed, and when they reach the Holy Spirit they say: who proceeds from the Father and the Son. Across the street, in an Orthodox church, the people say the same creed, and at the same spot they say: who proceeds from the Father. Same creed. Same Spirit. A difference of a few words in English, and in Latin, just one. That word has a long story. Today's word: filioque.

Filioque is Latin for and the Son. The Nicene Creed, as the early councils agreed it in Greek, said the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father. That echoes Jesus at the Last Supper in John's Gospel: "the Spirit of truth, which proceedeth from the Father." In the West, where the church prayed in Latin, churches came to add filioque. The English prayer book carries it: "Who proceedeth from the Father and the Son." Catholic and Anglican churches, among others in the West, have said it that way. Orthodox Christians say the creed without it, for two reasons. A creed agreed by the whole church shouldn't be changed by one part of it. And they speak of the Father as the one source within the Trinity. Western teachers answer that the word guards the bond between the Son and the Spirit, and point to the very same verse, where Jesus says of the Spirit, "whom I will send unto you from the Father." The Son sends; the Spirit proceeds from the Father. Orthodox teachers reply that sending in time is not proceeding in eternity. Each side leans on a different half. This one word became one of the disagreements in the long, painful parting between East and West, and it's still not settled. But in recent times the tone has grown gentler, with Catholic and Orthodox leaders talking it through patiently, and some Western churches leaving the word out when they pray alongside the Orthodox.

Say the line quietly in the Western form: I believe in the Holy Ghost, the Lord and giver of life, who proceedeth from the Father and the Son. Then say the Eastern form, stopping at from the Father, and notice what changes and how much stays the same. Hold in mind the people who will say each one this Sunday; if you pray, you can pray for both.
Filioque. Latin for and the Son: one word Western churches say in the creed and the Orthodox do not.
Your line: one word, long argument. These days, it's held more carefully. I'll be here tomorrow.

chat.says: Why do Orthodox churches leave out a word in the creed that other churches say?
options: They keep the creed as the councils agreed it, and see the Father as the one source.
They dropped it only to protest Rome, though they agree with what the word means.
They say the Holy Spirit doesn't come from God at all, only from the church.
chat.meaning: Orthodox Christians hold that a creed agreed by the whole church shouldn't be changed by one part, and they speak of the Father as the one source.

Nicene Creed.meaning: the creed the early councils agreed, first in Greek

Last Supper.meaning: Jesus's last meal with his friends, in John's Gospel

Orthodox.meaning: the churches of the East, which say the creed without filioque
